title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
This page is the end of Scholion 29 and Definition 30 of E449. Euler's aim in the paper is to show that a primitive root exists modulo every prime P.

Step 1. In §28 Euler showed, by repeatedly dividing out linear factors (Lagrange's theorem for polynomials mod P, in his form), that x^n - 1 ≡ 0 (mod P) has at most n solutions. The scholion clarifies that solutions are counted as residues: a and a+mP are one case, so only values 0 ≤ x < P are admitted.

Step 2. With this convention there can be fewer than n solutions. His example: x^5 ≡ 1 (mod 7) has only x = 1, and the other four roots 'quasi fiunt imaginarii'. This is correct, since gcd(5,6) = 1.

Step 3. He announces two claims. First, if n does not divide P-1, some solutions are always missing. Second, if n divides P-1, all n solutions are 'real', i.e. present mod P. The modern statement is that the number of solutions is gcd(n, P-1).

Step 4. For n = P-1 all P-1 nonzero residues are solutions, by Fermat's little theorem (§22).

Step 5. For n = P-1+k, x^n - 1 reduces to x^k - 1, because x^{P-1} ≡ 1. This is reduction of the exponent mod P-1; iterating it, together with the divisibility relations, gives the gcd.

Step 6. Definition 30 introduces 'proper cases' of x^n - 1: solutions that are not shared with any x^m - 1 for m < n. In modern terms these are residues of exact multiplicative order n, the primitive n-th roots of unity mod P.

The following pages (Corollaries 31-33, Problem 34) count proper cases: n-1 when n is prime, and an inclusion-exclusion over divisors in general. This gives φ(n) when n | P-1 and all roots exist. Applied to n = P-1, it yields φ(P-1) primitive roots, hence at least one.
errors: The claim 'quoties n est pars aliquota ipsius P-1 omnes solutiones sunt reales' (n | P-1 implies exactly n solutions) is only announced here ('ex sequentibus patebit'). It is the crux of the primitive-root existence proof. Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, art. 56, as I recall) judged Euler's demonstration in this paper defective, a gap usually located at this point. The statement can be proved by noting that x^n - 1 divides x^{P-1} - 1, which has exactly P-1 roots, and applying the at-most-degree bound to the cofactor; I am unsure whether Euler's later sections make this argument rigorously.
The reduction of x^{P-1+k} - 1 to x^k - 1 tacitly excludes x ≡ 0 (mod P). This is harmless because 0 is never a root of x^n - 1.

ideas.what: Counting solutions of x^n ≡ 1 mod P as residue classes; fewer than n roots possible (x^5≡1 mod 7 has one root)
ideas.modern_name: Number of n-th roots of unity in F_p equals gcd(n,p-1)
ideas.where_published: E449 (Novi Comm. Petrop. 18, 1774), also E262/E271 circle

ideas.what: n | P-1 implies x^n ≡ 1 has exactly n solutions
ideas.modern_name: Splitting of x^n-1 over F_p for n|p-1 (cyclicity of F_p^*)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss (first complete proof), stated by Euler and Lambert

ideas.what: Reduction of exponent modulo P-1 via Fermat
ideas.modern_name: Fermat's little theorem / exponent arithmetic mod p-1

ideas.what: Definition of 'casus proprii': solutions not common with lower exponents
ideas.modern_name: Elements of exact order n; primitive n-th roots of unity mod p (cyclotomic polynomial roots)

missed.claim: Euler describes the 'missing' roots of x^n-1 mod P as roots that 'quasi fiunt imaginarii', an explicit analogy between absent roots mod p and imaginary roots of equations. This is suggestive of Galois's 'imaginaires' (finite field extensions, 1830). It is a terminological anticipation, not a construction, and historians may already have noted it.
missed.quote: dum reliqui 4 casus quasi fiunt imaginarii
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A minor historiographical point on the prehistory of finite field extensions; no mathematical novelty.

deep.surprise_reason: Standard, well-documented content of E449: Lagrange-type root bound, gcd count announced, and the definition of exact order leading to φ(n) primitive roots. Gauss already discussed this paper. Only the 'imaginary roots' phrasing is mildly notable.
transcription_corrections: The page uses long s (e.g. 'ſint', 'ſaepius', 'ſolutiones') and 'quiualere' split across the line as 'ae-quiualere'. The transcription normalises long s, which is acceptable.
'praestet' in the image reads 'praeſtet' (partially garbled 'ſteι' in the scan); the meaning is confirmed.
